story_text.value:
Small Python (spy) is a small, embeddable Python engine written in C11. Pretty much like quickjs for javascript, it's for Python.

The entire Python core language features is full implemented with almost all builtins. No Lib/ is included except sys/gc that changes the interpreter behaviors.

Is missing Python stdlib a pain? Probably no. Host injected modules allows any language's ecosystem to be used in Python syntax. Check examples, you can build game by using Raylib, or build web server using Axum/Serde_python (using Rust crates).

Just copy `spy.h`, `spyc-*.c` into your project and use it as a C library. Or several bindings are provided for languages like Js, Python, Rust, Go. You can install via pip, npm, crate, go. Worker mode is recommended so that any issue would be contained in a subprocess.

It's fast. Well, not at the speed of Pypy because it's not JIT. But it's slightly faster than C Python in most benched cases.

Another good feature is compiling Python into a binary. You could use PyInstaller, but it's gonna be so large. Small Python's binary is small. A raylib + spy based PONG game is built at around 2MB.

It's using a full suite of tests: unittest, fuzz, sanitize, bench, TLA+ specs. Despite using C, agents are unable to spot a single segfault as of now. So that's pretty cool. :)

The roadmap aims to build it for agents: snapshot/resume between durable sessions, policy declaration so agents never shoot on your feet, etc.

It has been built for one week. I have a long Claude Code session running over several days with /remote-control using Opus 5.5.

Repo url: https://github.com/soasme/small-python Previous HN post: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50281226

story_text.value:
Hey HN Community!

I created checkOwners to solve a problem by many engineering teams: who knows your codebase, and what will happen when they go away?

This is an open-source, local-first tool which performs analysis based on Git history in order to find hidden knowledge risk in repositories.

It is able to recognize true experts, recognize out-of-date ownership definitions, find knowledge bottlenecks, propose review candidates, and model what would happen when contributors go away.

All the magic happens on your own local system without uploading source code or an LLM. It also works within GitHub Actions.

Try it: ``` pip install checkowners checkowners audit checkowners risk ```

Would appreciate any feedback from maintainers and platform engineers regarding the accuracy of Git history reflection of expertise and findings of risk analysis.

story_text.value:
A few days ago, I got OpenAI's email that Prism will be officially shutting down on January 1. Having written my last paper in it, I was quite disappointed since I've never really enjoyed typing LaTeX by hand for long periods. Also, when I updated my macOS recently, I started playing around with Apple's Foundation Models a bit (which I'm late on). So on Saturday I decided that, instead of studying for my midterms, my weekend project was going to be building a local version of Prism that used on-device Apple FMs.

It's an Overleaf-style editor with a PDF preview that compiles with TeX Live, and it installs TeX for you if you don't have it. To use the AI features, select text and press Cmd-K, and you can accept or reject the diff. If you have a handwritten formula that you want to insert, you can place your cursor where you want to insert and drop in a photo, which GLM-OCR turns into LaTeX locally since Apple's OCR doesn't handle math.

What was fun was testing out the capability of the models. Corollary uses SystemLanguageModel.default, which is Apple's general-purpose on-device model and the one built into macOS for Apple Intelligence. It's about 3B params with a 4,096 token context window on my M1 Max. When asked for plain text, it kept every \cite, \ref, \label and formula intact in 78 of 80 edits, but with structured output (@Generable) it went 0 for 20 because the JSON escaping eats the backslashes (\text comes back as a tab). While this limits capabilities like full document edits, you can already point it at Ollama or your own API key, and I'm sure the models will catch up soon.

Also, it needs an Apple silicon Mac, and the AI needs macOS 26 with Apple Intelligence. At this stage I don't have an Apple Developer ID yet, so the first launch needs System Settings > Privacy & Security > Open Anyway. Sorry about that. Please give it a try and let me know what bugs you run into or what the model struggles on!

Github: https://github.com/calvinyz/corollary

story_text.value:
Hi HN! We built nonce, an open-source tool that sits between personal AI agents (Muse, Grok, ChatGPT, Claude) and your personal data in Gmail, Calendar, Drive and more.

Today, if you connect Gmail to an AI agent like Muse, it can read your entire inbox. Whether on purpose or not, they can read far more emails than needed. This poses a huge data-privilege risk, in which personal data is accessed without limits.

With nonce, the AI will no longer hold your Google or Slack tokens. To read anything, it has to show its intent first:

User's question: When does my flight to Tokyo leave? Agent's justification: Need the airline confirmation email Agent's search query: from:united.com Tokyo Access needed: 10 minutes

If the justification and search query are reasonable, nonce issues a scoped token to the AI Agent. AI Agent can only query data using a token.

If something looks fishy, i.e the AI is acting on its own, wants too much, or wants sensitive emails like bank statements, medical results, or password resets. nonce sends you a notification to approve or deny.

By default, nonce denies massive crawling behaviors

How it works 1. nonce scores each search against your original question before running it, to ensure its relevance. 2. Every search is combined with the token's search. If the AI searches "bank statement", nonce runs (from:united.com Tokyo) AND (bank statement). It can narrow its access, but not widen it. 3. The token is scoped to that agent only, with a TTL for X minutes.

Limitations: nonce can't see your chat with the AI, so it can't prove you asked, which leaves a risk that the AI Agent can fake the intent. However, users can audit past accesses in nonce portal and identify these bypasses.

Give it a shot at https://github.com/roe-ai/nonce We'd love to hear what you think.

Website: https://anonce.io

story_text.value:
Show HN: An AI traffic guardrail

Building something based on 2 decades of support experience.

It's a guardrail for AI traffic where you can apply policies, redact PII and API keys, set model destinations, catch destructive actions before execution, etc.

The whole thing is built with Claude and can also be configured and troubleshot via Claude/AI tools (it acts as an MCP server).

It acts as a proxy for AI traffic. All you need is a Linux box (the Collector, where policy rules are applied) and a client app installed on the machine generating AI traffic to forward selected requests to it.

Everything is visible in the UI. Lots of customization, with user experience kept in mind throughout.

Happy to answer any questions!

story_text.value:
Quarter sits on top of the launcher client you already have. It grabs your library and hands every action back to the launcher, there's no login or password, no API key or data collection. Your client does everything else.

Quarter is just a fast shortcut to play your favorite games from the terminal you live in every day. That was my main mission when I created Quarter; just insert quarter, pick a game, press Enter.

Written in Go with Bubble Tea, reads Steam's own files on disk; game logos are drawn as pictures in the terminal using Sixel (terminals that don't support it will have a text fallback).

Steam today; Epic, GOG, EA and more launchers next.

Tested on Windows 11 with Windows Terminal. Did automated checks on Linux and Mac; but no tests as a real human with Steam installed, I appreciate the feedback a lot.

What launcher would you like next?

story_text.value:
I usually have many projects and terminals I’m working in so Crosswalk groups my work together and allows me to open a terminal (or another terminal app) in the correct folder/project quickly and label the tab (as well as add notes). I started on iTerm2 (which is great) years ago for my terminal manager, then found I spent too much time flipping between tabs once I started leveraging terminal agents like Claude Code and Codex so I built Crosswalk to improve visibility at a glance. It originally started as a web page, but then I moved it to an app so I had better control over notifications and sounds to let me know when work was done or needed me on one of the tabs.

Crosswalk shows which sessions are still working or sitting idle with an activity dot on the tab. It provides hotkeys to jump between tabs and groups quickly. Even if you're not using agents, you can still use it for your terminal work - I commonly leave active projects as groups on the left even if I not working in them right now. There's an MCP server so an agent can launch new tabs (and agents) - it's helpful when you need a lead agent to spawn long running agents (in visible tabs) and then monitor their status (running, stuck, needs user feedback) or compact their context at efficient times. There are other nice features like layouts to view multiple terminals at once and reopens terminals from last session. I spent a bunch of time iterating on the pty host (pseudoterminal host) so updating the app or closing and then reopening will restore the sessions.

This is a paid product you can trial for free. I created it to solve the multi agent bottlenecks so I use it daily, both personally and professionally. For Mac and Windows - Electron based.

story_text.value:
I spent the weekend with Claude assembling some pages for interactive exploration of a variety of basic DSP topics.

I have published the pages at https://dsp.gundy.dev/

My main goal, initially, was to build something for myself, as a way to refresh my memory and/or satisfy my curiosity on topics I love. My problem is that I find signal processing textbooks dry. Static diagrams and heavy math don't engage me very well, and I much prefer things I can interact with. As the pages started taking shape, I started thinking others might get some benefit too.

I've tried to keep the pages relatively light on math, except where it genuinely illuminates, and also keep the pages full of interactive examples. For example an in-browser acoustic modem is built up piece-by-piece and used to demonstrate modulation; multiple synths are playable with MIDI keyboards; many pages give you the ability to record your own samples and use them eg. for pitch shifting or compression or modelling your own guitar body in the physical modelling page. There's the ability to measure the SNR of your own room to determine its capacity to carry information, and much more.

I'm genuinely interested in any and all feedback - things that I could have covered better, other topics to include etc. I still have a roadmap of a number of things I'd like to cover, and I figured before I get too much deeper, it could benefit from some wider socialisation and feedback.

Also note: this is an ad-free hobby project and for the foreseeable future will remain that way.

All demos run in the browser only, no data is sent to, or processed by anything other than your own machine.

Thanks!

story_text.value:
Each creature in this data lab is a real text classifier. You put together a workflow, and the creatures execute it. Just set a stream of incoming messages and watch them work: one filters out the spam, another tags each message's mood, finally a router sends each message to the right bin, and anything it isn't sure about goes to review

The classifiers run entirely in your browser. It uses a 22.7M parameter model, int8 ONNX, about 10 ms a message, no API calls

Outside the lab, the creatures also evolve, chat, gossip, build huts, plot charts, count numbers, process and eat words, code and dream when asleep. You can also see their stream of consciousness, which they turn into thoughts that they tag. And when they are asleep, you can watch their dreams

There are a lot of ways of modifying or evolving the environment and the creatures, including adding elements from other websites, playing music and changing the weather

And if you want to change anything at all, talk to the Operator (or make it smarter), connect it to your Claude or OpenAI subscription, or setup your API key, or point it to a local model in Ollama or LM Studio, and you can edit the whole world via chat, without limits (get the code here: https://github.com/nicobrenner/id-le)

What else would you like the creatures to do?

PS: Happy Halloween

Outside the lab, the creatures also evolve, chat, gossip, build huts, plot charts, count numbers, process and eat words, code and dream when asleep. You can also see their stream of consciousness, which they turn into thoughts that they tag. And when they are asleep, you can watch their dreams

There are a lot of ways of modifying or evolving the environment and the creatures, including adding elements from other websites, playing music and changing the weather

And if you want to change anything at all, talk to the Operator (or make it smarter), connect it to your Claude or OpenAI subscription, or setup your API key, or point it to a local model in Ollama or LM Studio, and you can edit the whole world via chat, without limits (get the code here: https://github.com/nicobrenner/id-le)

What else would you like the creatures to do?

PS: Happy Halloween
